name: Sam Walsh

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the lead buyer for hand tools, fixings and fasteners at Ridgeway Trade Supplies, which sells to builders' merchants across the region. I'm up at six for a ride, then at my desk by eight with a coffee and my AI assistant open, which I use to sort the overnight quotes. Mid-morning I'm on calls with manufacturers about screw prices, and I get out to the warehouse most afternoons. I run a team of four, and Friday afternoons we review what we over-ordered.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like most about the job, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that the numbers have a story. A 2 per cent move on drill bits means someone in Germany has made a decision. What wears me out is the sheer volume: 11,000 product lines, and each one has someone calling about it. My wife Jo runs a GP practice, and she says I'm the only man who gets giddy over a new spreadsheet formula.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. I call this one "AI Plateau". If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a decent tool, nothing mystical. At work I'd say keep using it for the dull bits, and don't expect miracles. To friends I'd say, relax, it'll be like spreadsheets in the eighties: a big deal, but gradual.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd be fine. I've been using it daily for two years and it already saves me about a day a week. If it just stays that useful, that's plenty. I'm 58, senior and I know my range.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on, add small improvements and maybe hand the weekly forecasting to the tool entirely. I'd keep teaching my team the little tricks. And I'd begin planning for 63, which means a second pot of savings for travel and my bike trips.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Pleased, even. I'd have what I want, a good job that lets me finish on time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If little changes, what do you lose from having gone all in on these tools?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing lost. I picked tools that already pay their way, so if they don't improve, they still earn their keep. If I'd bet on a promise, I'd be sore.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What worries you, apart from AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The building trade. If construction slows, my customers slow, and my numbers drop whatever AI does. And Jo's practice is short of doctors, so she's always stretched. Home life is busy, but it's the good sort of busy.

say: I'd say it's a **decent tool**, nothing mystical, and will arrive gradually like spreadsheets did.
At work I'd say keep using it for the dull bits.
think: Privately I'm fine: it already saves me about **a day a week**.
My real exposure is the **building trade**, not AI.
do: Hand the weekly **forecasting** to the tool and keep teaching my team the small tricks.
Start a second **savings pot** for travel and bike trips ahead of 63.
feel: **Calm**, even pleased: a good job that lets me finish on time.
S0.quote: I picked tools that already pay their way, so if they don't improve, they still earn their keep.
fieldNote: His calm rests on **proven savings** from tools he already uses.
The risk he names is a building slowdown, which would hit his volumes.
Upbeat and informal, with a team-teaching instinct.

steps.text: Hand the weekly forecasting to the AI tool
Keep teaching the team small AI tricks on Fridays
Start a second savings pot for travel and bike trips

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. I call this one "Steady Disruption". If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the real deal, and the smart thing is to ride the wave. At work I'd say let's be the team that shows how to use it, not the team it's used on. Online I'd say expect some bumps, and let's help those who fall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, the reordering and price checks will be done by software. I've already built a script that does part of it. What's left is supplier talks, range choices and judging risk. That's probably half my job, and it's not safe forever, but I'm positioned well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd automate the routine buying properly this year, with our IT lot. I'd retrain my team to handle exceptions and supplier talks. And I'd start a small side project with a friend who's building buying tools for small merchants, because I know what they need.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, with a pinch of adrenaline. It's like a long downhill: exciting if you're ready for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the routine buying all goes to software, what's left in your job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Priya and Dan are the ones I'd back first. Priya's keen and Dan's good with people. The weaker links are Fiona, who's 59 and tired of change, and a new starter who's not found his feet. I'd talk straight to Fiona about what the job becomes and give her a choice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do for the four people in your team?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably judgement under uncertainty, and relationships. When a factory in Poland has a fire, someone has to decide what to do with 40,000 units on order. A machine can suggest, but I'd want a person who can ring the owner at nine at night.

say: I'd say the smart move is to **ride the wave** and be the team showing how to use it.
Online I'd say expect some bumps and **help those who fall**.
think: Privately reordering and price checks go to software, leaving **supplier talks** and risk, about half my job.
I'm positioned well, but it's not safe forever.
do: **Automate** routine buying this year with IT and retrain the team on exceptions and supplier talks.
Start a side project with a friend building **buying tools** for small merchants.
feel: **Calm** with a pinch of adrenaline, like a long downhill.
S1.quote: I'd want a person who can ring the owner at nine at night.
fieldNote: He treats change as **opportunity**, and has already built a script.
Honest about Fiona, who is 59 and tired of change, and about the limits of his own safety.
Side project grows from real knowledge of small merchants.

steps.text: Automate routine buying with the IT team this year
Retrain the team to handle exceptions and supplier talks
Start a side project on buying tools for small merchants

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. I call this one "AGI by 2028". If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's moving at a speed nobody planned for, and we'll need to be adult about it. At work I'd say let's focus on what's in front of us, and talk straight. Online I'd say governments should start with a safety net, now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, my job goes in two years, and so does Jo's, or at least half of it. She runs the practice: rotas, billing, the phones. A lot of that is thinking work that software can do. My wife Jo and I would both be in the line of fire, which is a lot of eggs in one basket.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The first month, I'd sit down with Jo and the numbers. We'd cut the spending, such as the new car, and top up the cushion. I'd look to move into a vendor role, where I'd be on the side that sells the tools. I'd also keep in with the union of buyers I'm in, and the local council on retraining.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Both our jobs are in the line of fire. We've got savings, but my brain does the maths all night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Jo's work is desk work too. How does that change this for the two of you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That we're both in the firing line, and that Hannah, our daughter, is a teacher. Teaching is safer, but the schools may change. We'd go through the lot together, and ask Ollie, who's a bike mechanic, to remind us that there are jobs where hands matter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the first thing you'd do in the first month?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Ridgeway for an early notice about what they plan. I'd call a couple of the software firms I already deal with and ask what a buyer who understands the trade is worth. And I'd tell my team, honestly, what I know.

say: I'd say it's moving at a speed **nobody planned for**, and we should be adult about it.
Online I'd say governments should start with a **safety net**, now.
think: Privately my job goes in two years, and **Jo's** practice work half goes too.

S2.quote: My wife Jo and I would both be in the line of fire, which is a lot of eggs in one basket.
fieldNote: His **anxiety** comes from two exposed earners, not his own skill.

steps.text: Cut spending and top up the cushion with Jo

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. I call this one "AGI by 2031". If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a decent runway if people use it. At work I'd start the planning now. Online I'd say it needs a national retraining push and not a series of pilots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd be happier. I'd be 63 and could glide out. And Jo, who's a bit younger, could see her job change gradually. Not nothing, but not a cliff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the first year to build up the side project with my friend, and put in a modest sum of my own, because I believe in it. I'd teach Priya everything I know about the range and the suppliers, so she has a head start. And I'd begin a part-time arrangement at Ridgeway near the end, if they'd have me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I'd know the date and could plan around it, which helps, but it's still there at the edge of the week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What changes about your choices with five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as I'd tell myself: learn the tools now, build a relationship with a few suppliers who like you, and have a plan B. Don't wait for the company to tell you what to be. Priya's quick, so she'd get it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want younger buyers like Priya to do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd also make Jo and me take a proper break each year, because stress eats judgement. If I'm going to be useful in a crisis, I need to be rested. It sounds small, but it's the sort of thing that matters.

say: I'd say five years is a **decent runway** if people use it.
Online I'd say it needs a national **retraining push**, not a series of pilots.
think: Privately I'm happier: I'd be **63** and could glide out.
Jo's job would change gradually, not fall off a **cliff**.

S3.quote: Learn the tools now, build a relationship with a few suppliers who like you, and have a plan B.

steps.text: Put a modest sum into my friend's buying-software project

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. I call this one "AGI by 2036". If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a long runway, and a gift. At work I'd carry on and keep up with the tools. Online I'd say we should use the decade to rebuild how we train young people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd be retired, probably cycling the Pyrenees. I'd be far from the stress, and I'd be curious rather than anxious. Jo may still be working, but she'd have had time to move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work to 63, and then start part-time advising for small merchants. I'd keep investing a bit each month in a world-wide fund and a share of my friend's firm. And I'd help Ollie open his own bike workshop, because he's good and it's hands-on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. I'd feel quite lucky.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years is a long time. What would you do with it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The best case is that the tools make everything cheaper, and that we share the gain with taxes and training. Hannah would be teaching, Ollie fixing, Jo working fewer hours, and me riding hills. I'd settle for that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the best case for a family like yours?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be a bit sad to leave the work behind, because I like it. But I'd also be glad, because it'd be a good time to stop. I'd keep in touch with the team, and go to their Friday reviews now and then, with cake.

say: I'd say ten years is a **long runway**, and a gift.
Online I'd say we should use it to rebuild how we **train young people**.
think: Privately I'd be retired, probably **cycling** the Pyrenees, and curious rather than anxious.
Jo would have had time to **move**.
do: Work to **63**, then advise small merchants part-time.

fieldNote: Decade makes him **optimistic**, grounded in a stable household.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year picture worries me most, because Jo and I would both be in the line of fire and there'd be no time. What would help is a proper safety net, retraining that's paid for by the firms that gain, and early warning from employers. Give me a few years and I'm happy to rebuild.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Just this. Being adaptive doesn't mean you're immune. It's easy for me because of timing and money. I've got a head start, but I'd not like someone to point at me and say, see, it's easy.

headlineQuote: Being adaptive doesn't mean you're immune. It's easy for me because of timing and money.
portrait: Sam is a **58-year-old** lead buyer of hand tools and fasteners at a trade distributor, who uses AI tools every day.
He is a cheerful centrist and keen cyclist who has already built scripts to automate part of his own job.
He is calm in most worlds, but **anxious** in the two-year one, since his wife's job is desk work too.
He doesn't blame anyone in particular, but wants a safety net and employers who give early warning.
Savings, an optimistic temperament and a hands-on son let him plan **side projects**, vendor roles and a gentle retirement.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** picture worries him most, since his wife and he would both be in the line of fire.
whatWouldHelp: A proper **safety net**, firm-funded retraining and early warning from employers.
